newsitem.title: CHINA: China sets up new body, looks to boost bankruptcy.
newsitem.headline: China sets up new body, looks to boost bankruptcy.

text.p: China has set up a new leading group to be responsible for bankruptcies, mergers and helping the jobless, taking a major step toward tackling a communist taboo that has long hampered reform of the state sector.

The State Council, or cabinet, had recently approved the establishment of the new group to handle nationwide bankruptcies, mergers and re-employment of those left jobless, the Xinhua news agency said on Sunday.

While the number of bankruptcies in China has accelerated in recent years, Beijing has shied away from a widespread use of the practice because of controversy over the closure of state-owned firms and creation of a pool of urban jobless.

Under the new rules, the leading group would be responsible for handling bankruptcies and mergers in cities that had been designated as pilots for the implementation of these methods of closing failed enterprises, Xinhua said.

A chief aim of the working group would be to ensure the re-employment of workers left jobless by bankruptcy or mergers to safeguard social stability, it said, referring to fears among the leadership of mass unemployment and unrest.

Under the new rules, pilot cities must work with the banks to decide whether the insolvent company should be declared bankrupt and report the amount of bad debts that must be covered by a central fund before a firm could proceed, Xinhua said.
China has said it would set aside 30 billion yuan ($3.6 billion) to cover bad debts of state firms this year, up from 20 billion last year.

An asset appraisal office approved by the central government administration would move into the firm, it said. If the land was owned by the state it should be handed over to a new owner after its value was independently appraised, it said.

Income from the sale of assets must first be used to re-employ jobless workers and if this money was insufficient then the local government must set aside a sum equivalent to three times the average annual salary of each worker, it said.

Management officials responsible for the bankruptcy of a company would be punished and those who had committed a crime would face charges, it said. Government officials responsible for the company may also face punishment.
This policy did not apply in non-pilot cities, nor could it be used in bankrupty of non-state firms, it said.
In mergers, the company that took over must take responsibility for all debts and workers, it said.

However, the company that handled a merger with a company that had lost money for the previous three years would be allowed to repay debts in installments over five years and without payment of interest, it said.

The number of bankruptices soared by more than 160 percent in China last year to exceed the total for the previous seven years, although experts have warned that many more insolvent firms wait in the wings.
A total of 6,232 firms declared bankruptcy in China last year, compared with 5,395 from 1989 to 1995.
The current rate of bankruptices was about 0.06 percent of China's estimated 10 million companies, including private and semi-state collective firms and the 100,000-strong state sector.
China has said reform of the state sector, with about 70 percent of enterprises making losses or hopelessly in the red, is a priority in 1997 but had yet to announce many specific reform policies.
